title: the gods who borrowed their glory
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hook: a friend's good news, and the Kena's gods who couldn't burn a straw
carry: all shining is brahman's light, borrowed
tomorrow: one person, alone at a window. so why does the verse say we?

segments.voice: Yesterday, shreyas over preyas: the good is worth choosing, varenyam. Worth choosing, but what? The answer opens the second line.

Somebody's good news lands in the group chat: early acceptance, dream school, a row of exclamation points. It's possible to be truly glad for a friend and still, for one second, feel a little dimmer. Priya had that second this week. It's a good second to meet the Gayatri's next words: bhargo devasya. The radiance of the god.

Bhargo means radiance, splendor. Its full form is bhargas, and before the d of devasya it turns to o. Devasya: of the god. So, the radiance of the god, and the first line's that finally lands. Now a story about whose shining it is. In the Kena Upanishad, the gods win a great victory, and they start to boast: this victory is ours, this glory is ours. Then a strange spirit appears in front of them, and they can't tell what it is. Agni, the fire, walks up: I can burn anything on earth. The spirit sets down one blade of straw. Burn this. Agni can't. Vayu, the wind: I can carry off anything. He can't move the straw. Then Indra goes, and the spirit vanishes, and in its place stands a radiant woman, Uma, daughter of the Himalaya. She tells him: that was Brahman. The victory you were proud of was Brahman's. That's the teaching: no one's shine is their own. The Katha Upanishad puts it in one line: everything shines after that one shining; by its light all this shines. Many teachers read the Gayatri's bhargo devasya that way: not my radiance, not yours, the god's. Which changes Priya's dim second. Anika's news isn't light taken from her. It's the same light, shining through someone else today.

segments.voice: If there's a lamp or a diya at home, light it and move it gently in a small circle, the way families do at arati, giving the light back to the one it came from. If not, count on your fingers people whose light you've seen by lately, and give each one a breath. Stop at five, or wherever the time runs out.
The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: bhargo devasya, the radiance of the god, a light nobody owns.

howItsDone: Teachers who explain the Gayatri often pause on bhargo devasya, the radiance of the god; some read it alongside the Kena Upanishad's story and the Katha's line that all things shine by one light. At arati, families wave a lamp before the deity, offering light back.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: bhargo devasya, the radiance of the god.

trapdoor: what you thought: the gods in the stories shine by their own power.
what it means: in the Kena, even fire and wind shine and move by Brahman; the Gayatri holds in mind the god's radiance.
what a scholar hears: bhargas is a neuter s-stem, -as becoming o before a voiced consonant; reading it with Kena 3–4 and Katha 2.2.15 is a teacher's reading, not the verse's grammar.
recall: shreyas over preyas: the good is worth choosing
of Savitr: greeted with water at sandhya

chat.meaning: In the Kena Upanishad the boasting gods learn their victory was Brahman's. Many teachers read bhargo devasya the same way: the radiance is the god's, so a friend's shine takes nothing from yours. It promises no result.

tie.story: In the Kena Upanishad, the boasting gods couldn't burn or move one straw, and Uma told Indra their victory had been Brahman's.

tie.you: whose light have you been measuring yourself against?

notes: Gayatri word by word: bhargo devasya. Grammar stated: bhargas (neuter s-stem), -as becoming o before voiced d; devasya as genitive singular in -asya. Confirm wording for learners.
The script avoids the deva/div ('shining') etymology and descriptions of Savitr's form from other hymns.
'Two lamps in one room don't dim each other' is the writer's image, offered as an application, not a teaching of the text; the voice says the verse promises no result.
